title: Preface
summary: The text is front matter of 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed' by James McAndrew, published by U.S. Air Force Headquarters. It includes a cover note on a solarized image from a U.S. Air Force film of Project HIGH DIVE experiments (Figure 37, page 34), plus Library of Congress cataloging data (subjects: UFO sightings in Roswell, New Mexico), and Government Printing Office sales and ISBN details.

title: Congress Cataloging-in-Publication Data
summary: Front matter of 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed' by James McAndrew (1997). Includes Library of Congress cataloging-in-publication data: subject heading for UFO sightings and encounters in Roswell, New Mexico; LC call number TL789.5.N6M33; Dewey 001.942; ISBN 0-16-049018-9. Also contains U.S. Government Printing Office sales notice (Superintendent of Documents, Washington, D.C.) and title-page fragments.

title: Foreword
summary: Foreword by Air Force Secretary Sheila E. Widnall on the Roswell Incident, a New Mexico event of the 1940s central to American folklore. The Air Force helped execute the GAO's tasking to uncover all records on it, aiming to declassify documents and consolidate them for public review. This volume follows The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction (July 1994), adds material and analysis, and reflects on the Air Force's 50th anniversary and its personnel.

title: Guide For Readers
summary: Front matter guide to the complete U.S. Air Force Roswell Report submitted to the Secretary of the Air Force. Describes two sections (alleged events at two rural New Mexico locations; activities at Roswell Army Airfield Hospital), appendices covering test equipment launch/landing locations (Project Mogul/Excelsior), sworn statements from in-person interviews (Appendix B, with privacy redactions), and witness transcripts presented by UFO theorists (Appendix C), plus a bibliography and a reference to the 1995 published version.

title: The Author
summary: Author bio: Capt. James McAndrew, Air Force Declassification and Review Team; coauthor of The Roswell Report (1995), first Air Force work on the Roswell incident; worked on Gulf War Air Power Survey declassification; DEA/HIDTA service. Table of contents: flying saucer crash and alien body claims; crash sites, scenarios, research methods; high altitude balloon dummy drops and operations; witness accounts of USAF activities; reports of bodies at Roswell Army Air Field hospital; nurse and pediatrician; aircraft accidents; high altitude research projects; notes; appendices with dummy launch locations, witness statements (Clouthier, Coltman, Fulgham, Gildenberg, Jorgeson, Kaufman, Kittinger, Lutz, Madson, Nordstrom).

title: Interviews
summary: The text is a table-of-contents style index listing oral-history interviews with page numbers: Gerald Anderson (p. 187), Glenn Dennis (p. 197), Alice Knight, Vern Maltais, and James Ragsdale, with some unnumbered page references (213, 214, 215). It contains no substantive content beyond these names and page numbers.

title: Selected Bibliography of Technical THe Tables

2.2 Fatal Air Force Aircraft Accidents by Year
summary: Front matter and table of contents of a document on the Roswell AAF/Walker AFB incident. Lists a selected bibliography of technical tables (pages 221-225). Section One: Table 1.1 compares testimony to actual Air Force equipment and procedures for launching and recovering anthropomorphic dummies (p. 69). Section Two: Table 2.1 lists persons described and periods of service at Roswell AAF/Walker AFB (p. 91); Table 2.2 lists fatal Air Force aircraft accidents by year at Walker AFB, 1947-1960 (p. 93); Table 2.3 analyzes Air Force aircraft accidents in the vicinity of Walker AFB by year (p. 94).

title: Figures
summary: A list of figure captions from a book about the Roswell incident and high-altitude research. Section One covers the Roswell report, debris and radar target images, anthropomorphic test dummies (Sierra Sam, Excelsior, Project High Dive), military vehicles, the Viking and Discoverer balloon and spaceprobe projects, and balloon launches at Holloman AFB. Section Two covers personnel, Walker AFB facilities, Kittinger's jumps, and UFO-related magazine articles.

title: Introduction

nodes.title: Introduction (intro)
nodes.summary: The text introduces the July 1994 Air Force report on the Roswell Incident, which concluded that 1947 debris came from Project Mocut, a classified-then-declassified balloon-borne acoustic detection program, not an alien craft. It states that later research attributes alleged alien bodies to anthropomorphic test dummies carried on high-altitude balloons and to unrelated Air Force accidents: a 1956 KC-97 crash and a 1959 manned balloon mishap. It also notes that the bodies claims emerged decades later from second- and third-hand accounts, and that UFO proponents misdated events.

nodes.title: SECTION ONE Flying Saucer Crashes and Alien Bodies
nodes.summary: Explains the Roswell Incident's alleged alien bodies, which turned a flying saucer story into a claimed best case for extraterrestrial visitation. A 1994 Air Force report attributed the 1947 events to Project Mogul, an acoustic detection balloon train with radar targets. Initial confusion at Roswell AAF was resolved, and from 1947 to the late 1970s the story was mundane. Body claims emerged later from second- and third-hand anecdotes gathered decades afterward, often via newspaper solicitations. Figures show Mogul balloon train components.

summary: Introduces the July 1994 Air Force report on the Roswell Incident, which attributed 1947 debris to Project Mogul, a balloon-borne acoustic detection program, not an alien craft. Later research ties alleged alien bodies to anthropomorphic test dummies on high-altitude balloons and to unrelated Air Force accidents (1956 KC-97 crash, 1959 manned balloon mishap). Body claims arose decades later from second- and third-hand accounts, and UFO proponents misdated events. Covers the Mogul balloon train components and how the story stayed mundane until the late 1970s.

title: Harassed Rancher ‘Saucer’ Sorry He
summary: Describes the 1947 Roswell incident: rancher W. W. Brazel found debris (tinfoil, rubber, paper, tape, sticks) on his Lincoln County ranch in June 1947, reported it to Sheriff Wilcox, and Army officers took the pieces; he said it was not a weather balloon. Also covers scientists Charles Moore and Bernard Gildenberg, who linked the event to Air Force balloon projects and were dismissed by UFO authors Berliner and Friedman, who promote a 'crash' cover-up theory and seek witnesses for their book 'Crash at Corona'.

title: Authors seek UFO witnesses
summary: Describes Fig. 8, a 1992 Socorro newspaper solicitation for flying saucer crash witnesses that drew former Air Force scientists' responses, which were dismissed. Figs. 9-10 profile Duke Gildenberg and Charles Moore, who ran Air Force balloon work tied to the Roswell Incident. Authors Friedman and Berliner seek witnesses to 1947 crashes for their book Crash at Corona, with contact details and New Mexico meeting stops. The text notes Roswell accounts are poorly documented, outlines the single original debris field site near Foster Ranch, and describes two later alleged crash sites with alien body claims, with a map in Fig. 11.

title: The Scenarios
summary: Explains that UFO enthusiasts use complicated scenarios to reconcile multiple Roswell crash sites with one craft. The actual Project Mogul balloon train landing about 75 miles northwest of Roswell in July 1947 lends credibility. 'Bodies' claims emerged only after 1978, erroneously linked to Mogul retrieval. Common scenarios: a damaged craft touched down, left debris, then flew to a final crash site; bodies were taken to Roswell AAF for autopsy, then shipped to Wright-Patterson AFB or elsewhere for deep-freeze storage.

title: Research Methods
summary: The text describes Air Force research into Roswell-related reports of bodies. A 1994 report found no evidence of a recovered extraterrestrial craft or crew, after reviewing millions of pages and interviewing released personnel. It states the bodies claims were linked to Project Mogul only after 1978, that the balloon train could not carry passengers or hazardous materials, and that no 1947 events supported the claims. Many accounts were eliminated, leaving working hypotheses about real but detailed events, two similar crash sites, and a separate hospital account.

title: Common Threads
summary: Describes Roswell-area 'crashed saucer' testimony: witnesses in rural New Mexico find a crashed aerial vehicle, see strange 'beings,' then military convoys arrive and order them to leave. Common details include the aliens' four-fingered hands, bald heads, and gray one-piece suits, plus vehicle types (wrecker, six-by-six, weapons carrier). Accounts are judged independent, though dates are uncertain and some witnesses suggest dummies or experimental planes.

title: The Research Profile
summary: Describes the Air Force research profile for Roswell-related sightings: an unusual-looking activity seen from a distance, of unknown date, in two rural New Mexico areas, involving aerial vehicles with four-fingered bald dummies in gray suits, recovered by military personnel and vehicles. Missiles, drones, and aircraft are ruled out (too far from White Sands, no dummy programs, geographic constraints). High altitude research balloons remain plausible: they carried anthropomorphic crash-test dummies from May 1950 onward, which could be mistaken for aliens. Figures show example dummies and a 1970s-era NHTSA safety-belt ad featuring dummies.

title: Test Dummies Used by the U.S. Air Force
summary: Traces the history of U.S. Air Force test dummies: early rope-and-sandbag 'Dummy Joe' parachute testers from World War I onward, then anthropomorphic dummies from 1944 (Ted Smith Co.) and the 1949-1952 Sierra Sam and Alderson models developed with John Stapp for ejection-seat testing. Also covers 1953-1959 high-altitude balloon and aircraft drops over New Mexico and Ohio (Project Excelsior, Hick Dive), and the dummies' link to the Roswell Incident.

title: Anthropomorphic Dummy Launch and Landing Locations
summary: Describes a historical document on Project Excelsior/High Dive era anthropomorphic dummy balloon launches and landings near Roswell, NM, including a debris field and a 'crash site' about 75 miles northwest of Roswell, White Sands Proving Ground, Holloman AFB, and El Paso. It cites 29 launches and mapped landing locations keyed to Appendix A, sourced from U.S. Air Force aeromedical test records. It notes alleged UFO sightings at some sites, and that Capt. Joseph Kittinger's 1960 record high-altitude parachute jump at 102,800 feet followed the dummy tests.

title: A Cover-Up?
summary: Counters cover-up claims: Air Force anthropomorphic dummy and human-subject projects at Holloman AFB were unclassified and publicized via books (Kittinger's The Long, Lonely Leap; Simons' Man High), National Geographic, Life, Collier's, Popular Mechanics, Time, MAD, and a 1956 film. Excerpt of Kittinger's record 102,800-ft parachute jump: high-altitude balloon gondola, stabilization lanyard, and photo caption from the December 1960 National Geographic, plus magazine cover figures.

title: Dummy Drop Procedures

nodes.title: Dummy Drop Procedures (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes Air Force high-altitude dummy drop tests (30,000-98,000 ft) from balloons, with dummies in standard flightsuits and parachute packs carrying accelerometers, pressure transducers, oscillographs and cameras during free-fall. Covers the Project Excelsior-style gondola releases, recovery by Holloman AFB Balloon Branch crews using wreckers, six-by-six trucks, weapons carriers and aircraft, and visibility aids like smoke, pigment and bright canopies plus $25 reward notices. Also includes photo captions of recovery vehicles and Stapp rocket sled tests.

nodes.title: The Bravest Man
nodes.summary: Biography of Col. John Paul Stapp, the 'bravest man' who rode a rocket sled to 632 mph in 1954 and endured over 42 g of deceleration. Covers his education, Air Force career, acceleration/deceleration research, safety innovations (belts, ejection systems, airbags, test dummies), balloon projects, Mercury astronaut support, awards, and 1991 National Medal of Technology. Also covers lost and damaged test dummies from 1955 high-altitude balloon drops at Holloman AFB, including a lost-equipment memo, dummy transport methods, and figures noting the four-finger detail linked to Roswell alien accounts.

nodes.title: On one occasion northwest of Roswell, a local woman
nodes.summary: Describes Air Force high altitude balloon dummy drops in 1957 research (WADC Technical Report 57-477). A woman northwest of Roswell found what looked like a human embedded head-first in a snowbank near a landing site and became hysterical, believing the dummy was dead. Anthropomorphic dummies dropped by high altitude balloons met the research profile. Review of balloon operations explained other sightings of odd objects in New Mexico. Holloman balloon branch launched about 2,500 balloons since 1947, including the June 4, 1947 flight later tied to the Roswell Incident. Figures show insulation bags used for dummies, a 1972 Viking-related balloon launch from Roswell, and NTIS report sources.

summary: Covers Air Force high-altitude dummy drop tests (30,000-98,000 ft) from balloons, with instrumented dummies in free-fall and recovery by Holloman AFB crews using visibility aids and reward notices. Profiles Col. John Paul Stapp, the rocket sled pioneer (632 mph, 42+ g), his safety innovations, awards, and lost 1955 test dummies. Describes a 1957 Roswell-area sighting of a dummy in a snowbank and how balloon operations explain other sightings, including the 1947 flight tied to the Roswell Incident.

title: On the Threshold of Space
summary: Describes the 1956 Twentieth Century Fox film 'On the Threshold of Space,' based on Holloman AFB Air Force aeromedical projects (High Dive/Excelsior balloon experiments and Col. John P. Stapp's high-speed sled tests), starring Guy Madison, John Hodiak, and Dean Jagger, filmed on location with real equipment and dummies later mistaken for aliens. Also covers a 1990 Unsolved Mysteries Roswell segment hosted by Robert Stack, who attended the 1956 premiere. Includes figure captions: lobby card, publicity photo, and sled test recreation.

title: High Altitude Polyethylene Research Balloons
summary: Covers the 1946 invention of polyethylene high-altitude research balloons by Charles B. Moore for Project Mogul, contrasting them with rubber weather balloons: they reach about 200,000 feet, carry payloads from pounds to tons, and hold stable level flight because they are launched with excess capacity. Early balloons were 7 feet across; modern ones can be football fields long. The text also covers 1950s flying-saucer misidentifications from Holloman AFB, including a 1953 London UFO sighting, and the later addition of transponders and strobe lights.

title: High Altitude Balloon Payloads
summary: Describes high altitude polyethylene balloon payloads flown from Holloman AFB, New Mexico, from the late 1940s through the 1980s: simple radio transmitters, dummies, satellite components, and NASA probes. Covers experiments in space biology, meteorology, air sampling, Project 119L reconnaissance, aluminum-laminated balloons used as radar missile targets from 1955, links to Roswell accounts, 1958 manned flights, 1960 satellite component tests, and Discoverer nosecone and capsule photos.

title: High Altitude Balloons and America’s First Satellite
summary: Describes Holloman AFB high altitude balloon tests in 1960 that evaluated Discoverer satellite components before Discoverer XIII recovered the first orbited object on August 11, 1960, nine days ahead of the Soviets. Also covers balloon qualification tests of Surveyor, Voyager-Mars, Viking, Pioneer and Galileo probes, and 1966-67 and 1972 Roswell balloon launches of saucer-shaped Voyager and Viking test vehicles, which may have influenced Roswell UFO accounts.

title: CENTER

nodes.title: CENTER (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes Holloman Balloon Branch activities: 1960s low-altitude experimental tethered balloons flown in New Mexico canyons, one of which (a March 1965 'Vee' balloon) resembles a drawing of an alleged alien craft in a UFO book. Covers today's reduced Air Force high-altitude balloon program (SMC/TE, OL-AC), its scientific uses, and worldwide launch sites. Explains that alleged UFO recovery crews were likely Holloman balloon recoveries in targeted Roswell-area zones, guided by meteorologist Bernard Gildenberg's control techniques.

nodes.title: Interaction with Civilians
nodes.summary: Describes Air Force Balloon Branch interactions with rural New Mexico civilians: allegations of intimidation are rejected; recoveries were coordinated with local police and landowners, crowds were common, and staff explained the flights as scientific studies. Confusion arose in the 1970s-80s when recovery trucks were mistaken for drug smuggling. Also covers figures of balloon equipment, unusual payloads, and comparison of witness accounts with Project Hicu Dive and Excelsior dummy flights.

summary: Covers Holloman Balloon Branch activities: 1960s low-altitude tethered balloons flown in New Mexico canyons, including a March 1965 'Vee' balloon resembling a UFO-book drawing. Describes today's reduced Air Force high-altitude balloon program (SMC/TE, OL-AC), its scientific uses, and worldwide launch sites. Explains alleged UFO recovery crews were likely Holloman recoveries near Roswell guided by meteorologist Bernard Gildenberg's techniques. Also covers civilian interactions: intimidation allegations rejected, recoveries coordinated with police and landowners, crowds common, flights explained as science. 1970s-80s recovery trucks mistaken for drug smuggling. Mentions balloon equipment, unusual payloads, and comparison with Project Hicu Dive and Excelsior dummy flights.

title: “Crash” Site 1

nodes.title: Assessment
nodes.summary: Describes the alleged 'crash' site 1 north of Roswell, based on an interview with witness James Ragsdale (who has since died) by author Donald Schmitt. Ragsdale, in two sworn statements, described two different sites many miles apart. He recalled camping with friends, seeing something in the sky, and finding the next morning a craft partly buried, with bodies or dummies that were under five feet long. Army personnel arrived with trucks, a wrecker and vehicles and cleaned up the area. The assessment argues his account matches anthropomorphic dummy recoveries from Projects High Dive and Excelsior, with confusion likely from distance and time.

nodes.title: If the
nodes.summary: Describes Air Force high-altitude balloon and anthropomorphic dummy programs: parachute failures during early free-falls from up to 98,000 feet caused dummy limbs to separate; a witness's remote-control and cover-up remarks; Balloon Branch procedures for cleaning landing sites to maintain community relations and avoid livestock and property claims, including cattle ingesting polyethylene balloon scraps; and vehicles (wrecker, six-by-six, weapons carrier, 1947 Ford, pickup) matched to 1950s recovery and launch equipment.

nodes.title: “Crash” Site 2
nodes.summary: Analyzes the alleged 'crash' site 175 miles northwest of Roswell (San Agustin Plains, NM), supported by two secondhand accounts (Alice Knight, Vern Maltais, recounting eyewitness Grady Barnett's description of hairless, four-fingered 'beings') and one firsthand account (Gerald Anderson, who as a five-year-old saw 'plastic dolls,' a 'blimp,' and military recovery). The author concludes these descriptions match Holloman AFB high-altitude balloon program anthropomorphic dummies, vehicles, aircraft, and procedures, and that claims of threats and secrecy are unsupported. Includes figures.

summary: Covers the alleged 'crash' site 1 north of Roswell, based on witness James Ragsdale's two differing sworn accounts of camping, seeing a craft, and finding under-five-foot bodies or dummies; Army cleanup followed. The author ties this to Projects High Dive and Excelsior anthropomorphic dummy recoveries. Also covers Air Force balloon and dummy programs: parachute failures, cleanup procedures, and matching vehicles. Analyzes 'crash' site 2 near San Agustin Plains, supported by secondhand and firsthand accounts, which the author links to Holloman balloon program dummies.

title: Summary

nodes.title: Summary (intro)
nodes.summary: Argues that UFO 'crash' accounts near Roswell were actually descriptions of Project High Dive and Excelsior high-altitude balloon launches and recoveries of anthropomorphic dummies. Witness similarities corroborate this. Sites are hard to pin down; Ragsdale's shifting testimony, and the San Agustin Plains account likely confused with San Agustin Pass/Peak near the White Sands and Jornada ranges. Supported by test records and photos.

nodes.title: Comparison Procedures
nodes.summary: A comparison table relating witness testimonies about the alleged 1947 Roswell incident to Air Force equipment and procedures. Witnesses (Anderson, Ragsdale, Maltais, Kaufman, Knight) described 'aliens' with hairless bodies, four fingers, gray one-piece suits, and a crashed 'craft' with cables and metal boxes; the Air Force explanations are anthropomorphic dummies (Alderson, Sierra Sam), high-altitude balloon payloads, parachutes, and tape-secured instrumentation. Also covered are witness descriptions of military vehicles (weapons carriers, M-35 and M-246 trucks, ambulances, pickups, fuel trucks, cars, a jeep with generator), aircraft (L-20, C-47, observation planes), and cleanup and reward procedures, with corroboration between Site 1 and Site 2 noted.

summary: Argues that Roswell 'crash' accounts were actually Project High Dive and Excelsior balloon launches and recoveries of anthropomorphic dummies, supported by witness similarities, shifting testimony (Ragsdale), and possible San Agustin Plains confusion with nearby geography. A comparison table maps witness claims (hairless 'aliens', four fingers, gray suits, cabled craft, metal boxes, military vehicles, aircraft, cleanup and reward procedures) to Air Force explanations (dummies, balloon payloads, parachutes, tape-secured instruments), noting Site 1 and Site 2 corroboration.

title: Reports of Bodies at the Roswell AAF Hospital

nodes.title: Reports of Bodies at the Roswell AAF Hospital (intro)
nodes.summary: Explains that Roswell AAF hospital references appear in most 'crashed saucer' claims, mainly from W. Glenn Dennis, a mortician whose undocumented 1989 recollections of alien bodies there are uncorroborated. His key claims came from unidentified mystery witnesses, and Air Force researchers found the dates, events, and people grossly inaccurate for July 1947.

nodes.title: The Account
nodes.summary: Summarizes W. Glenn Dennis's 1989-era account of alleged events at Roswell AAF hospital, July 7-9, 1947: a mortician received calls about child-sized caskets, transported an airman, saw strange bluish wreckage and MPs at military ambulances, was threatened by a redheaded officer, and later met a nurse who described mangled small bodies being autopsied. The nurse was reportedly shipped out and later reported dead. Theorists claim alien autopsies and crash debris; Air Force research found major date and detail errors, and the events match Project Mogul retrieval.

nodes.title: 2.1 “Missing” Nurse and the Pediatrician
The “Missing” Nurse
nodes.summary: Examines the alleged 'missing nurse' and unidentified pediatrician from the Roswell AAF hospital claims. Morning reports and personnel records show no nurse was transferred on the alleged July 8-9, 1947 dates; the only nurse reassigned was on July 23 by normal rotation. The name 'Naomi Maria Selff' appears nowhere in military records. Eileen M. Fanton, the only one of five July 1947 Roswell nurses who closely matches the description, is identified as the likely basis for the claims, and her unannounced September 1947 departure for medical treatment explains the hospital's privacy-protective responses.

nodes.title: The Pediatrician
nodes.summary: The text describes claims by a witness, Dennis, that a hospital pediatrician was involved in Roswell-related events. Records identify the only pediatrician who moved to Farmington, N.M., as Frank B. Nordstrom, who served at Walker AFB 1951-1953 as Chief of Pediatric Services; he denies meeting Dennis or recalling the events. Pharmacist Charles Clouthier confirms Nordstrom was the area's sole pediatrician from 1954 to about 1970. The text then covers the 1948 Aztec, N.M. fictional flying-saucer story, Scully's 1950 book Behind the Flying Saucers, and con-men Silas Newton and Dr. Gee, whom J.P. Cahn exposed in True magazine articles (1952, 1956).

Covers claims about a 'missing' nurse and unidentified pediatrician tied to Roswell AAF hospital. Records show no nurse transfer on July 8-9, 1947; the name Naomi Maria Selff is absent from military records. Eileen M. Fanton, a closest match, is likely the basis; her September 1947 unannounced medical departure explains hospital privacy responses. Witness Dennis's pediatrician claim is addressed: Frank B. Nordstrom, sole pediatrician in Farmington area, denies it. Also covers the 1948 Aztec flying-saucer hoax, Scully's 1950 book, and con-men Silas Newton and Dr. Gee exposed by J.P. Cahn.

summary: Covers W. Glenn Dennis's late-1980s uncorroborated claims of alien bodies at Roswell AAF hospital (July 1947), sourced from unidentified witnesses; Air Force research found the dates and details inaccurate. Dennis describes child-sized caskets, bluish wreckage, MPs, a threatening officer, and a nurse who reported mangled bodies, later reported dead; events match Project Mogul. Also addresses the 'missing' nurse (Naomi Selff absent from records; Eileen Fanton likely basis), a denied pediatrician claim, the 1948 Aztec hoax, Scully's 1950 book, and cons Newton and Gee exposed by Cahn.

title: Descriptions of Other Air Force Members
summary: Excerpt from an Air Force review of the Roswell incident witness claims. It finds official records show no nurses missing at Roswell AAF in July 1947. The witness's details (airman rank, black sergeant, 'big redheaded colonel', and nurse 'Captain Wilson' nicknamed 'Slatts') are shown to match later periods. Colonel Lee Ferrell commanded the Walker AFB hospital 1954-1960. Lucille Slattery, nicknamed 'Slatts', arrived a month after the event and is 5'3". Maj. Idabelle Wilson, 5'9" and thin, served 1956-1960 and denied the claims. The witness likely confused later events with 1947.

title: Results of Missing Nurse and Pediatrician Research

nodes.title: Results of Missing Nurse and Pediatrician Research (intro)
nodes.summary: Analysis of the Roswell missing nurse and pediatrician claims. Research found no matching nurse named Wilson or Naomi Selff, and identified the pediatrician as Capt. Frank Nordstrom, who arrived in 1951. Nurses Idabelle Wilson (1956-60) and Lucille Slattery (arrived Aug 1947) are checked against the account. All July 1947 nurses are accounted for. Table 2.1 maps witness descriptions to actual personnel and service periods, suggesting the witness may be mistaken about timing.

nodes.title: The Research Profile
nodes.summary: Describes a possible 1947-1960 Walker AFB hospital event tied to the New Mexico 'crashed saucer' reports: mangled black small bodies with a strong odor placed in body bags, two non-hospital doctors doing preliminary autopsies, a large-headed body sent to Wright-Patterson AFB, a redheaded captain or colonel, an ambulance holding bluish-purple inscribed wreckage, and heightened security. Linked to high-altitude balloon anthropomorphic dummy findings.

nodes.title: 2.2 Aircraft Accidents
nodes.summary: Covers a 1947-1960 review of Air Force aircraft accidents near Walker AFB, New Mexico, which identified eight fatal accidents (B-29, C-47, KB-29, T-33, B-47, KC-97, KC-135 types) with locations, dates, and fatalities. Researchers checked whether victims were burned, transported to Walker hospital, or autopsied. Only the June 1956 KC-97 accident met all three criteria for the 'black bodies' investigation, supported by records and witness interviews.

summary: Research on Roswell-related missing nurse and pediatrician claims found no nurse named Wilson or Naomi Selff; the pediatrician was identified as Capt. Frank Nordstrom (arrived 1951), and nurses Idabelle Wilson and Lucille Slattery were checked, with all July 1947 nurses accounted for. Table 2.1 suggests the witness may be mistaken on timing. It describes a possible 1947-1960 Walker AFB hospital event (black bodies, autopsies, Wright-Patterson transfer, security) linked to high-altitude balloon dummy findings. A 1947-1960 review of eight fatal Walker AFB aircraft accidents found only the June 1956 KC-97 crash met all criteria for the black bodies investigation.}

title: Fatal KC-97 Aircraft Mishap
summary: On June 26, 1956, a KC-97G of Walker AFB's 509th Aerial Refueling Squadron crashed 8.8 miles south of the base during refueling training after a propeller failure caused a fuel tank puncture, fire, and loss of control. All 11 crewmen died; no ground casualties occurred. Remains were identified at the 4036th USAF Hospital, then moved to a refrigerated commissary due to odor. An identification specialist from Wright-Patterson assisted, and a Roswell pathologist autopsied three victims. Remains were then sent to next of kin.

title: the KC-97 Mishap; Account
summary:
theKC-97Mishap
Account

title: Comparison
summary: The text compares a 1956 KC-97 crash at Walker AFB (Roswell) with Dennis's UFO-related account, finding many similarities: mangled black small bodies in body bags, a strong odor, two 'doctors,' and a redheaded colonel. It notes that UFO theorists have historically exploited real aircraft accidents, citing the 1947 Kelso B-25 hoax, a 1948 'alien' photo with aviator sunglasses, and the 1948 Franklin, Ky. P-51 crash, which was actually a high-altitude balloon. It describes autopsy findings, the funeral home link, Air Force mortuary procedures, the hospital commander Col. Ferrell, and identification specialist George Schwaderer. It also covers the pathologist Dr. Alfred Blauw and AFIP's absence, concluding the unusual details likely stem from uninformed observers and secrecy restrictions.

title: Continuing Research
summary: The text describes a research shift to explain unexplained profile portions: a redheaded captain, wreckage and an ambulance at Walker AFB hospital, heightened security, and a shipment to Wright-Patterson AFB. Earlier research covered high altitude research balloons launched near Roswell since the late 1940s. By 1960 many balloons, some carrying anthropomorphic dummies, were recovered near Walker AFB and Roswell, but the hospital and medical involvement made them unlikely explanations, so focus moved to manned Air Force high altitude balloon flights of the 1950s and early 1960s. A photo shows Simons, Winzen, and Kittinger examining a gondola model.

title: Manned Balloon Flights

nodes.title: Manned Balloon Flights (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the manned balloon projects MAN HICH (1957-1958) and Excelsior (1959-1960), which made six high-altitude flights with no injuries, heavy media coverage, and none near Roswell. Records and interviews confirmed only these six. Numerous low-altitude training flights at Holloman AFB, N.M., included several mishaps with injuries, notably a May 21, 1959 accident northwest of Roswell at Walker AFB. Analysis suggests that accident resembled the reported events.

nodes.title: US. Air Force Manned High Altitude Balloon Projects
nodes.summary: Covers U.S. Air Force manned high altitude balloon projects (1957-1962) that bridged the gap to manned spaceflight. Describes Project Man High I (Kittinger, Simons; 1957 flights to ~101,500 ft), its link to Mercury, Project Excelsior (three Kittinger parachute jumps, record 102,800 ft free-fall), and Project Stargazer (1962 astronomy flight to 86,000 ft, only one of four planned flights). Includes a flight table and notes the end of the balloon era once rockets and Mercury took over.

nodes.title: Low Altitude Balloon Training Missions
nodes.summary: Describes Air Force Project EXCELSIOR and STARGAZER high altitude balloon work: Capt. Joseph Kittinger's role, the 1958 Man High I balloon accident that injured Winzen and Schock, and the 1959 low altitude training flights at Holloman AFB with backup pilots Fulgham and Kaufman. Covers the May 21, 1959 landing mishap that injured Fulgham and Kittinger, the medical safety protocols, and the post-accident handling at Walker AFB.

nodes.title: 2.4 Comparison of the Hospital Account to the Balloon Mishap
nodes.summary:
2.4 Comparison of the Hospital Account to the Balloon Mishap
The balloon mishap near Roswell on May 21,1959 provides the probable explanation for some of the remaining elements of the incident profile—the redheaded captain, the unusual security at the hospital, the wreckage in the rear of an ambulance, and one portion of the accounts of “aliens” at the Roswell AAF hospital.

summary: Covers U.S. Air Force manned high-altitude balloon projects (1957-1962) bridging to spaceflight: Man High I (Kittinger, Simons; flights to about 101,500 ft, link to Mercury), Project Excelsior (three Kittinger parachute jumps, 102,800 ft free-fall record), and Project Stargazer (1962 astronomy flight to 86,000 ft). Notes six high-altitude flights without injuries, many low-altitude Holloman training flights with mishaps, and the May 21, 1959 Walker AFB accident near Roswell, which likely explains elements of the Roswell hospital account.

title: The “Redheaded Captain”

nodes.title: The “Redheaded Captain” (intro)
nodes.summary: The text argues that the 'redheaded captain' in Roswell accounts is likely Capt. Joseph W. Kittinger, Jr., who was at Walker AFB hospital after a balloon mishap. Kittinger wanted to leave quickly to avoid an accident investigation that could endanger Project Excelsior, and he sought to limit publicity; his supervisor Col. Stapp agreed. The text denies that he threatened anyone, citing multiple witness statements and his composed character. It then gives Kittinger's biography: his career as a test pilot, Project Man High I, Excelsior high-altitude jumps, Project Stargazer, Vietnam combat and POW service, later ballooning achievements, decorations, and honors. Figures show Kittinger in 1963 and a communications technician's ambulance.

nodes.title: The “Wreckage” in the Rear of the Ambulance
nodes.summary: Describes wreckage in the rear of a Walker AFB ambulance linked to a 1959 balloon accident. Covers alleged 'alien hieroglyphics' (actually stenciled lettering on an equipment rack), steel panels painted Air Force blue mistaken for escape pods, and debris that was the broken polyethylene balloon. Identifies the ambulance as a converted Holloman Balloon Branch communications vehicle and the ramp as the Bldg. 317 dispensary.

summary: Argues the 'redheaded captain' in Roswell accounts is likely Capt. Joseph W. Kittinger, Jr., at Walker AFB hospital after a balloon mishap. Gives his biography: test pilot, Man High I, Excelsior jumps, Stargazer, Vietnam POW service, ballooning feats, decorations. Describes Walker AFB ambulance wreckage from a 1959 balloon accident, the 'hieroglyphics' (stenciled rack lettering), Air Force blue panels mistaken for escape pods, and the broken polyethylene balloon debris.

title: Additional Security at the Walker AFB Hospital
summary: Describes heightened security at Walker AFB hospital when injured balloon crew (Capt. Fulgham) arrived in 1959. Covers SAC 6th Bombardment Wing context, surprise inspection practices, security escort and skepticism from hospital staff, verification via Col. Stapp, and Fig. 24-26 captions. Also covers Capt. Kittinger's association with Dr. J. Allen Hynek on Project Bluebook and StarGazer, Hynek's later UFO endorsement, and Holloman balloon origins of the Roswell incident.

title: The Alien at the Hospital
summary: Describes the 1959 balloon accident involving Capt. Dan D. Fulgham and Kittinger, near Roswell, New Mexico, and the resulting alien-like appearance attributed to a forehead hematoma. Covers the clinical record cover sheet (traumatic hematoma, May 21, 1959, Holloman AFB hospital), photos of Fulgham at Wright-Patterson AFB after blood aspiration, Kittinger's 'big blob' and 'grotesque' descriptions, Fulgham's unawareness of his appearance, his public exposure in the hospital including military wives, and a note that the alien-hospital sighting claim is unverifiable.

title: “Bodies” with Large Heads and Wright-Patterson AFB, Ohio
summary: Describes the aftermath of Fulgham's 1959 balloon mishap: UFO theorists' 'large-headed bodies' claim at Wright-Patterson AFB is likely a misreading of his return there. He was hospitalized at Holloman, then flown to Wright-Patterson on a C-131 arranged by Kittinger; he could not see and was led off the plane, and his wife screamed, not recognizing him. He returned to work and flying with no lasting effects, retiring as a colonel in 1978 after Korean and Vietnam combat tours and space program work.

title: Summary
summary: The Roswell AAF hospital reports of 'bodies' were grossly inaccurate and likely stemmed from actual Air Force mishaps. Official records show the alleged 'missing nurse' was never missing, and the pediatrician did not arrive at Walker AFB hospital until 1951, four years after the alleged incident. Fundamental errors and similarities to real mishaps show the most credible 'Roswell Incident' account is not extraterrestrial and is unrelated to July 1947 events.

title: Conclusion
summary: The text concludes an Air Force review of the 'Roswell Incident.' It finds the flying saucer and alien claims are a mix of real 1950s Air Force tests (high-altitude balloons, escape systems) distorted by UFO proponents, plus distorted references to members killed or injured in service. No evidence of saucers, aliens, or cover-ups was found. The Air Force defends its record and its duty to challenge exploitation of tragedies.

nodes.title: Transcript of Interview with Gerald Anderson* Alleged firsthand witness to “Crash Site” Two (allegedly 175 miles northwest of Roswell) (intro)
nodes.summary: An interview transcript, excerpted from a 1993 Fund for UFO Research video, in which Gerald Anderson recounts a childhood trip to the Plains of San Agustin near Socorro, New Mexico, to find agates. He describes finding a crashed silver disc about 35 feet wide embedded in a ridge, with four non-human beings: two dead, one badly injured, and one unharmed. He details their appearance (about four and a half feet tall, large heads, black almond eyes, bluish-white skin, no hair, slit mouths, three-fingered hands), their silver-gray one-piece suits, a gash in the craft, its cold metal, and an acetone-like smell. He tells of touching a body, feeling a mental burst of emotion from one creature, and of others arriving: a professor-led archaeology group, a man resembling Harry Truman, and military personnel who cleared the site amid panic.

nodes.title: Like he was scared?
nodes.summary: A witness recounts a confrontation with military personnel after reaching a site: a red-headed officer named Armstrong threatened people with shooting and warned them to stay silent. A soldier shoved the uncle, Ted, who struck back, prompting rifles to be cocked. Dr. Buskirk and others intervened. The group was herded up an arroyo, held without searches, and escorted to the highway, where they saw a large military presence including a landed C-47, ambulances, trucks, and MPs in light khaki uniforms. They were denied water, told to go to Socorro, and the witness last saw Buskirk arguing with the officer.

summary: Excerpt of a 1993 Fund for UFO Research interview with Gerald Anderson, who as a child visited the Plains of San Agustin near Socorro, New Mexico, to find agates. He describes finding a crashed silver disc about 35 feet wide with four non-human beings (two dead, one injured, one unharmed), detailing their appearance, suits, craft, and smell. Later arrivals included an archaeology group, a Truman-like man, and military personnel who cleared the site. He recounts a confrontation with a red-headed officer named Armstrong, a shove between soldiers and his uncle Ted, denial of water, and escort to the highway past military vehicles.

title: Transcript of Interview with W. Glenn Dennis* (Alleged firsthand witness to events at the Roswell AAF hospital)
summary: Transcripts of Roswell-related interviews. W. Glenn Dennis, a Roswell funeral home ambulance worker, recounts July 1947 calls from the base mortuary officer, taking an injured airman to the base hospital, and meeting a nurse who showed him a drawing of small bodies and later vanished (transferred, then a returned letter marked deceased). He describes seeing debris in ambulances, being confronted by a redheaded captain and MPs, his father's early-morning visit after sheriff Wilcox's call, lost personal files, and criticism of Friedman and Randle's accounts. Alice Knight and Vern Maltais relay secondhand accounts of a crash site 175 miles northwest of Roswell with alien beings. A brief James Ragsdale entry closes the text.

title: Transcript of Interview with James Ragsdale* (Alleged firsthand witness to “crash site” north of Roswell)
summary: Transcript excerpt of a 1993 interview with James Ragsdale, who claims to have seen a crash site north of Roswell in 1947. He describes camping nearby with a woman, finding half-buried debris with carbon-paper-like plastic/metal that could be folded and would not hold its shape, and seeing bodies or dummies about four to five feet long. He describes Army trucks, MPs, and a cleanup of the site, and says the area stayed cordoned off for weeks or months. He speculates that two craft collided, or that the government used dummies in an experiment, and notes he showed the debris to a friend. Location is given as roughly 30 to 40 miles northwest of town via Highway 48.

The text also covers a car wreck with the debris locked in the trunk, a stolen car, a house break-in about eight years earlier (1985), and the murder of Mrs. Ragsdale's brother.
